elements.text: Sudden severe leg pain at rest with any of the following in the leg: numbness, weakness, pallor, no pulse, acute limb ischaemia likely

elements.section: Give urgent attention to the patient with peripheral vascular disease and any of:
elements.text: Leg pain occurring at rest, ulcer or gangrene on leg, critical limb ischaemia likely

elements.section: Give urgent attention to the patient with peripheral vascular disease and any of:
elements.text: Pulsatile mass in abdomen with abdominal/back pain or BP < 90/60: ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm likely
Manage urgently:
If acute limb ischaemia likely, refer urgently.
If critical limb ischaemia likely, discuss same day urgency of referral with specialist.
If ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm likely, avoid giving IV fluids even if BP < 90/60 (raising blood pressure may worsen the rupture). Refer urgently.
PERIPHERAL VASCULAR DISEASE (PVD)

• Peripheral vascular disease is characterised by claudication: muscle pain in legs or buttocks on exercise that is relieved by rest. Leg pulses are reduced and skin may be cool, shiny and hairless. • Refer the patient newly diagnosed with peripheral vascular disease for specialist assessment.

Treat the patient with peripheral vascular disease • Help patient to manage CVD risk 144. Advise brisk exercise for 30 minutes at least 3 times a week (preferably daily). Advise patient to pause and rest whenever claudication develops. • Give rosuvastatin 10mg daily regardless of cholesterol level. If patient develops muscle pain/cramps, reduce dose to 5mg daily. If no improvement and not on LPVr/ATVr/DRVr switch to simvastatin 10mg at night or discuss with specialist. Avoid if pregnant or breastfeeding. • Give aspirin 150mg daily for life. Avoid if peptic ulcer, dyspepsia, kidney or liver disease.

• Refer to specialist at diagnosis (start medication and exercise while waiting for appointment) and if pain interferes with activities of daily living after 3 months of medication and exercise. • Review 3 monthly until stable (coping with activities of daily living and able to work), then yearly.

Advise the patient with peripheral vascular disease • Advise patient to keep legs warm and below heart level (especially at night), and to avoid decongestant medications that may constrict blood vessels. • If patient smokes, encourage to stop 164. Support the patient to make a change 199. • Advise patient that physical activity is an important part of treatment. It increases the blood supply to the legs and may significantly improve symptoms. • If < 55 years (man) or < 65 years (woman), advise first-degree relatives (parents, siblings, children) to have CVD risk assessment 142.
Assess the patient with peripheral vascular disease
Assess When to assess Note
Symptoms Every visit • Ask about chest pain 24 and symptoms of stroke/TIA 152. Manage other symptoms as on symptom pages. • Document the walking distance before onset of claudication.
Mental health Every visit If stress, anxiety or low mood 98.
Cancer Yearly Check if eligible for cancer screening or if early symptoms/signs of cancer 194.
BP Every visit If known hypertension 149. If not, and BP ≥ 140/90 148.
Legs and feet Every visit Check for pain, pulses, sensation, deformity, skin problems. For foot screen and foot care education 81.
Abdomen Every visit If pulsatile mass felt, refer for assessment for possible abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Fingerprick glucose At diagnosis, then yearly If known diabetes 145. If not known diabetes 19.
